task.title: Box sizes
task.shortdesc: By default a box is as wide as the box that contains it and as high as its content. Use the size properties to give a box another size, or to limit its size.

step.cmd: Set the width and the height

info.p: The width and height properties set the preferred size of a box. Their initial value is auto, which lets layout choose the size. A size can be a length, such as 200pt, or a percentage of the size of the containing block.
The properties inline-size and block-size do the same by the direction of the text: the inline size is the width and the block size is the height in horizontal text.
The box-sizing property tells what a width or a height measures:

ul.li: content-box is the initial value. The size is the size of the content. The padding and the border are added outside it.
border-box makes the size include the padding and the border, so the content is smaller.

info.p: This note is 200pt wide from the outside of one border to the outside of the other. With content-box, it would be 228pt wide.

image.alt: Two boxes with the same width of 200pt. With content-box the content is 200pt wide and the padding and border add to 228pt. With border-box the whole box is 200pt wide and the content is 172pt.

step.cmd: Size a box from its content

info.p: These keywords can replace a length in any size property:

ul.li: min-content is the smallest size that the content can have without overflowing. For text, it is the width of the longest word.
max-content is the size that the content has when nothing wraps.
fit-content is the available space, but not less than min-content and not more than max-content. fit-content(limit) uses a length or a percentage as the available space.
stretch makes the margin box fill the available space.
contain fills the available space and keeps the aspect ratio of the box, if it has one.
calc-size() calculates a size from another size. calc-size(auto, size / 2) is half of the size that auto gives.

info.p: Minimum and maximum sizes limit the preferred size. min-width, min-height, min-inline-size and min-block-size take the same values as width. Their initial value is auto. max-width, max-height, max-inline-size and max-block-size take the same values, and none too, which is their initial value. When a minimum is larger than a maximum, the minimum wins.
This illustration fills the line, but is never wider than 40em.

step.cmd: Place the content in a box that is taller than its content

info.p: When you give a box a height and its content is shorter, the content is at the top of the box. The align-content property moves the content as a whole:

ul.li: normal is the initial value. It puts the content at the top, as start does.
center puts the content in the middle, with the same space above and below it.
end puts the content at the bottom.
space-between and stretch put the content at the top, and space-around and space-evenly put it in the middle, because a box has a single block of content to place.
baseline puts the content at the top and last baseline at the bottom. In a table cell they align the lines of the cells instead, as Turn elements into a table explains.

info.p: The top and the bottom are the start and the end of the direction in which the lines follow each other. In vertical-rl text, the start is the right side of the box and the end is its left side.

Content that is taller than the box stays at the top and runs out of the bottom, so that its start is never lost. Write unsafe before the value, as in unsafe end, to align the content as you ask anyway: with unsafe end it runs out of the top. In a box whose overflow is hidden, scroll or auto, the content is aligned as you ask unless you write safe before the value, so with end the end of the content is what shows.

fig.title: The values of align-content in a box with a fixed height

image.alt: Five boxes of the same height. With normal and start the content is at the top, with center in the middle and with end at the bottom. A content taller than its box stays at the top with end and runs out of the bottom; with unsafe end it runs out of the top and ends at the bottom of the box.

info.p: With min-height instead of height, the content is aligned when it is shorter than the minimum height.
A value other than normal makes the box a new formatting context: the top margin of its first child stays inside it, and its floats stay inside it.

A box that breaks across pages is aligned as it would be in one piece. The space before the content goes on from page to page, and the content stands where it would stand in the unbroken box. When that space reaches the end of a page, the content starts on a later page, and content that cannot be split and does not fit after the space goes to the top of the next page.

step.cmd: Place a block across its containing block

info.p: A block normally fills the width of its containing block. The justify-self property places it along the line instead: start, center, end, self-start and self-end, and left and right, which always name those sides. A block without a width then becomes as wide as its content, and a block with a width keeps it. normal and stretch keep the block as it is.

The start and the end follow the direction of the text: in a right-to-left block, end is on the left. A block wider than its containing block is aligned as you ask, so center makes it stick out on both sides; write safe center to keep it at the start instead.

fig.title: The values of justify-self on blocks

image.alt: Four blocks in a containing block. The block with normal fills the line; the blocks with start, center and end are narrower and stand at the left, in the middle and at the right.

info.p: Auto margins come first: margin-inline: auto centers the block, whatever its justify-self. With fixed margins and a fixed width, the block is aligned between its margins.

The initial value, auto, takes the justify-items of the parent, so you can set the alignment of all the children of an element at once. justify-items: legacy center also passes the alignment on to the grandchildren and further, as long as their own justify-items is legacy. Floats, and the anonymous blocks that hold loose text, are not aligned.

The size property sets the width and the height. min-size and max-size set the two minimum sizes and the two maximum sizes. They take one or two values, and one value applies to both. With two values, the width comes first.

The aspect-ratio property gives a box a ratio between its width and its height. When you set one of the two sizes, CSSMedia calculates the other. Write the ratio as two numbers separated by a slash, such as 16 / 9, or as one number. A single number is a ratio to 1. The initial value is auto, which uses the ratio of an image if the box has one.
This frame is 320pt wide and 180pt high.

step.cmd: Give a size to a box that ignores its content

info.p: A box with contain: size is sized as if it were empty. Use contain-intrinsic-width, contain-intrinsic-height, contain-intrinsic-inline-size, contain-intrinsic-block-size, or contain-intrinsic-size for both, to give it the size that it should have instead. They take a length, or none, which is the initial value.
